F07.title: Checkout Blocks nativo e tipos próprios
F07.gate: Todos os tipos não-file da V1 possuem renderer homologado ou restrição explícita coerente; nenhum modo é anunciado além do testado.
F07.detail: WCCS-036 delivered the Blocks adapter. The additional-fields API of the installed WooCommerce accepts exactly text, select and checkbox — a private, unfiltered array — and the adapter's declared list is compared in the proof against the list the platform itself answers when it is asked to register a type it does not have, because there is no API to ask and a comment is not evidence. date is named by section 8 and by the task's own acceptance, and is not there: it is refused with the code needs_controlled_component naming WCCS-037, instead of being registered as text and discovered by a customer. Three policies follow from the same discipline. Locations are resolved and never guessed: billing and shipping are one address location, contact and account are contact, order is order, and a field whose section is not published is refused rather than defaulted to order, which is the family of mistake WCCS-018 had to fix. Storage the platform does not perform is refused: a native field is persisted on the order, so a definition declaring scope none or scope customer is refused with storage_not_native, which is ADR-0001's one-authority rule applied before the field exists. And a select with no options is refused, because a select with no options has nothing to choose from. The third piece is the one that makes WCCS-035 stop being a library: a representable visibility rule is registered as the native required *and* the native hidden — the negation of the same schema — which together mean 'required exactly when it is shown', and which WooCommerce honours, since is_required_field returns false for a hidden field. The proof reads both rules back out of WooCommerce's own registry and validates them with WooCommerce's own meta-schema. A rule that cannot be expressed natively does not stop the registration: the field is registered without it and the reason is reported, which is ADR-0008 pointing the other way, and the difference between 'the platform cannot express this' and 'the merchant cannot use this field'. WCCS-037 delivered the components the Blocks checkout cannot get from the platform. The classification became a function of the definition rather than of the type, and that is the task's most useful decision: a mask is part of what the merchant configured, the native text input cannot carry one, and a document typed into it would be stored unformatted and refused by the server — so a masked text is rendered by this plugin even though its type is native. Without it the acceptance's 'presets mascarados' half would not have reached the Blocks checkout at all, and the proof is what showed it: the first version published the textarea, the radio and the date and left the masked field in the missing list. The components are controlled and hold no copy of the value, because a component with its own state survives a re-render holding a value the checkout does not have — the duplication the phase gate names. The mask taught the one real integration constraint: a mask and a React controlled input do not coexist, because React assigns value directly to the element and bypasses the mask's listener, so the element owns the text and the value is reported on every accepted change; the checkout still owns the value through one rule — the value from outside is written into the element only when the element is not the one being typed into. The temporal fields use the native date, time and datetime-local inputs rather than a custom widget, because the browser already supplies the picker, the keyboard and the customer's format. A type with no component returns null and names itself instead of drawing a text field that would collect something the store cannot save. The payload travels through one inline script written before the bundle, and the registration seam is injected rather than imported: the bundle finds the checkout API, builds the elements and hands them over, answering no_blocks_checkout_api rather than pretending — because a field that is drawn but whose value goes nowhere is worse than a field that is not drawn. WCCS-038 delivered the Store API integration, which is what a controlled field needs to exist at all: a field this plugin draws does not exist as far as WooCommerce is concerned, so nothing carries its value to the server until a namespace does. The namespace is typed by what the component produces rather than by what the customer sees — a multi-select is an array with string items, a checkbox is a boolean — and that is what makes the route validate the shape before any of this plugin's code runs; a schema saying string for everything would be a decoration. Only the fields the renderer draws and whose storage is native are declared, from the same document and the same classification, so a field cannot be drawn without being postable or postable without being drawn. Validation and persistence share one hook, woocommerce_store_api_checkout_update_order_from_request, and not by convenience: throwing from it is documented to prevent checkout, which is the only way an extension can stop a payment from this side, and sharing the hook is what removes the intermediate state where the order advanced without its values. The refusal carries a prefixed code, the rule's own message and the field that produced it, so the block can render the message against that field; the message is escaped the way WooCommerce escapes its own route errors, and the code and field identifier deliberately are not, because they are machine-readable and escaping a code changes the contract the block matches on. The pipeline is the classic one, so a rule cannot mean one thing in one checkout and another in the other, and the trusted context builder was generalised from ClassicConditionContext to CheckoutConditionContext for exactly that reason: the same questions are answered by the same WooCommerce objects in both checkouts, and a second implementation would have disagreed the first time one of them was edited. Retrying a submission leaves one meta row and one payload, byte for byte, which the proof shows by saving the order between two identical submissions the way the route does. The proof also caught itself: its first run died silently calling a method that does not exist — the third such death this session, and the reason the sweep reads every harness's exit code rather than only its RESULT line — and it left its published option behind, so it now establishes its state instead of inheriting it. WCCS-039 delivered the capability matrix on the publishing surface. It is deliberately not the incompatibility report under another name: that report answers whether something would not be honoured, in the vocabulary of warnings, while the matrix answers what each checkout does with each field whether or not any of it is a problem — four columns is honoured by the classic checkout and not applied in the Block one, which is a fact to decide with rather than a defect to fix. Both travel in the same response under separate keys so the interface cannot merge them by accident, and the proof asserts they are not the same object. Four families are resolved per field: core (what can and cannot be done to a WooCommerce field, including the drift the inventory can detect), width (the twelve column grid that honours twelve and six, the class this plugin applies for four and three, and the Block checkout's own layout, which ignores the number), section (the logical location and where each adapter puts it, with the classic checkout's lack of a contact step named as the reason a contact field is drawn with the billing address) and type (provided, limited or unavailable). The Block answers come from BlocksAdapter::mode_for() — the same function that decides what gets registered — because a second table here would be the interface promising something the checkout does not do, which is what section 8 and the phase gate both forbid. The proof found a defect that no test would have: the core drift check read the inventory as a map keyed by field identifier, and CoreFields returns a flat list, so the condition was always true and the branch could never fire. It surfaced because the proof printed its own observed value — field=0, an index where an identifier belongs — which is what every assertion in this project prints its detail for. WCCS-040 delivered the Blocks lifecycle, and it is deliberately not the classic mechanism: the classic checkout is replaced by server-rendered fragments and WCCS-025 solved that by capturing before the AJAX call and restoring after it, while here React unmounts and mounts subtrees whenever the address, the shipping method or the payment method changes and what survives a remount is state that was never in the component. So the values live in one store owned by the page's lifecycle and a component is a view over it, rendering what the store holds and reporting what the customer typed. Nothing reads the DOM to recover a value, and that is asserted rather than promised: the last spec spies on the MutationObserver constructor and asserts it is never built, because a module that recovered values by watching the document would make every other spec pass while reading back whatever React last rendered. The hidden-value policy is applied on both sides for the same reason it exists on one: a field a rule hides either keeps what was typed or loses it, and the two checkouts have to answer alike — which required the policy to travel in the payload, so BlocksRenderer now publishes it with each field, discard by default. The jsdom suite pins the acceptance word by word: the value survives an unmount and a fresh mount, survives a re-render, is recorded on every keystroke through a harness that renders what the store holds, and hiding discards or preserves according to the declared policy. The suite also corrected itself once: the typing spec first expected 'h' and received 'i', because a controlled input without the client writing the value back resets on every keystroke — which is exactly the failure a checkout that kept the value in the component would have.

defects_found_and_fixed: The typing spec asserted 'h' after typing 'hi' and received 'i': the controlled input had no client writing the reported value back into the store, so React reset it between keystrokes and the second keystroke reported the whole text again. The spec now renders what the store holds and writes back what the component reports — which is the shape the checkout itself uses, and the failure it would have had.

The hidden-value policy did not travel to the page at all, so a client-side store had nothing to apply when a rule hid a field: the server applied discard or preserve and the page could only guess. Found while writing the lifecycle, fixed by publishing the policy with each field, defaulted to discard the same way the definition defaults it.

F08.title: Upload privado nos dois checkouts
F08.gate: Upload privado permanece privado, cota e retenção aplicadas, download só com autorização.
F08.why_gate_is_open: All five tasks are complete and the gate is met at every seam, which is why it is still marked open: the gate's clauses are about behaviour a store depends on — a private upload staying private, a quota and retention applied, a download only with authorization — and each is proven on rows, files and the route, but no browser has uploaded anything and no checkout has bound an upload to a real order. There is also a finding this phase cannot resolve from inside the plugin: this store's private directory is served over HTTP, so the feature is off here and the blocker UPLOAD-PRIVACY-ENV is the first thing to fix before a single byte is accepted. One deliverable is recorded as missing rather than claimed: the Block checkout's upload field.
F08.way_forward: Two things close it and neither is implementation: the environment configuration recorded in UPLOAD-PRIVACY-ENV, and the browser work in WCCS-063 and F12, where a customer uploads a document, places an order and downloads it through the policy. The Block checkout's upload field belongs with that same integration work. F09 may proceed meanwhile: it depends on the presentation layer, not on this observation.
F08.detail: WCCS-041 delivered the storage and the operational table, and the environment answered a question the task was built to ask. The private directory is a sibling of `uploads` rather than a child of it — the uploads path is published by design, and every protection for a file inside it is either obscurity or a rule the server may not be reading — and it carries the denial files for the three common servers. The proof then did the only thing that settles the question: it wrote a file and asked the site for it over HTTP through the site's own address. This store's nginx served it, 200 with the contents, because .htaccess is an Apache file and index.php is only consulted when a request reaches PHP. The finding is recorded in section 4.1 of the threat model and as the blocker UPLOAD-PRIVACY-ENV, and the product's conduct is the acceptance's second clause proven on a real unprotecting environment: the feature is off and it says why an operator can act on it. The observation is cached so a storefront request does not probe, and a stored refusal is never turned into an approval by the cache expiring — only a fresh probe can re-enable the feature, which is why the diagnostic surface can forget the record on demand. The operational table exists because the questions the subsystem asks are about rows: which file belongs to which session, how many bytes an owner has spent, when a temporary expires. An option would load one serialised array to answer about one upload, and a quota cannot be counted from an option at all. It is installed on activation and on every boot, because an update over the files never runs the activation hook, and its existence is asked of the database rather than assumed from the version option — a table can be dropped after the option is written, and a subsystem that trusted the option would fail on its first insert instead of reporting itself unavailable. Paths are the security-relevant half and are asserted: the stored name is generated rather than taken from the browser, a name that tries to leave the directory gets no address, and a stored path is validated against the directory before it is read, so a row cannot make a download read /etc/passwd. The task also caught a stale assertion in another phase: the preview proof asserted that no wccs_ option existed anywhere, which was true when it was written and stopped being true when this task gave the plugin state of its own to keep — rewritten to say what it means, that the preview stored nothing of its own. WCCS-042 delivered the endpoint and the tokens, and inherited the previous task's finding as its first assertion: on this store every upload is refused before the file is read, with the environment named as the reason, because a store whose private directory is public must not spend a byte finding out whether the file was acceptable. The rules are what an upload feature usually gets wrong and are proven as rules: the declared extension and the browser's content type are not evidence — a shell script named document.txt with type text/plain is refused on what finfo detects — and the quota is a sum over what the owner has stored, because a limit per file does nothing about a thousand small ones. Ownership is a session identifier generated on the server and kept in the session, deliberately not the customer id: a guest has none, a logged-in customer may check out from two devices, and an identifier two checkouts share is one that lets either read the other's documents. The repository makes that a property of the query rather than of a check somebody has to remember: every method that answers 'whose is this' takes the token and the owner. The proof demonstrates it the only way it can be demonstrated, by asking as somebody else: another session receives not_yours and no record, a token that does not exist receives unknown_token — two different answers on purpose, because collapsing them would hide a probing attempt inside an ordinary mistake — and another session cannot remove the file either. One separation the proof forced: is_uploaded_file() was in the service and made it unusable outside a real request, which the harness discovered with eight failures; it moved to the controller, which is the boundary and the only place with a request, so the service checks what the file *is* and the boundary checks that it was uploaded at all. WCCS-043 delivered the upload component and the state machine both surfaces share, and the acceptance lives in the machine rather than in the views: progress, cancel, remove, retry, accessible refusals, and 'sem upload duplicado' understood as four different accidents rather than one. Two clicks on the button are one record and one transfer, because the same document chosen twice would otherwise leave two copies with one referenced; a retry landing while the first attempt is still travelling is refused by a state and not by a disabled attribute, which anyone rendering the button can undo; a file the store already accepted is never re-sent, because the token is the store's record that it holds those bytes; and two different documents that happen to share a name are both accepted, since identity is name, size and modification time. Casting the acceptance as one clause would have covered one of the four. The classic checkout has no file type in WooCommerce's field API and does not need one: an unknown type reaches the woocommerce_form_field_{type} filter, which is the documented seam, and ClassicUploads renders a labelled input with the markers the bundle looks for plus a sentence saying uploads are unavailable when the store cannot keep a file private. Giving the classic adapter that type broke six proofs from earlier phases, all legitimately: five used file as the example of a type the classic checkout cannot render and now use a structural type, and four enumerate the storefront's hooks exactly and had to name the new one. That is the honest cost of changing a capability, and the assertions were updated to say the new truth rather than weakened. The sweep also caught something worse than a stale assertion: enabled() observed when there was no observation, and observing is an outbound HTTP request to the store's own address — with the component calling the gate, that put a network round trip in front of the checkout and let a slow server decide whether a customer can upload a document, and it made building the page's data a write. The gate now reads and never observes; an environment not yet observed is simply not available yet, and the observation happens when the diagnostic surface or an administrator asks for it. WCCS-044 delivered the order binding and the download policy. The binding is one UPDATE and every guarantee comes from the statement rather than from the code around it: atomic because there is no read-then-write window, idempotent because order_id = 0 is part of the condition so a retry matches nothing, and owned because owner = the session is in the same condition and cannot be forgotten at a call site. The reply is a count for that reason: the first call says how many it bound and the second says zero, and neither is an error — which is what makes a client that submits twice safe. A forged token belongs to nobody, so it binds nothing and the order is placed without it. One function decides who may read a file: the session that uploaded it, the customer the bound order belongs to, or staff who manage the store, and the refusal is the same for every reason including a token that does not exist, because telling those apart would let anyone enumerate which handles are real. The comparison is hash_equals and not a prefix test, and an upload with no owner is readable by nobody. Files leave through one controller that reads them from the plugin rather than handing them to the web server — the point of the storage is that the server cannot serve them, so that is the only place the policy can be applied — as an attachment with nosniff and a private no-store cache header, because a document a customer uploaded is not a page. The task also paid a maintenance debt it was the second to incur: four proofs enumerate the storefront's hooks exactly, and both this task and WCCS-043 changed that list, so it now lives in one shared file the four read. The assertion is still a deliberate inventory, but a new hook no longer has to be remembered in four commits. WCCS-045 delivered retention, which is the task that stops a store accumulating documents nobody will ever read. An upload has three lives and each has its own rule: a temporary one has no order to belong to and expires, an effective one belongs to an order that exists and stays while it does, and an orphaned one belongs to an order that is gone and goes with it — the case a store that deletes test orders collects without noticing. A failed upload is not a case at all, and saying so is part of the rule: a refusal writes neither the file nor the row, so a cleaner that looked for failures would be looking for rows that never existed. The clause that is easy to claim and hard to hold is 'cleanups podem repetir', and it is asserted rather than promised: the second run removes nothing and leaves the table as it found it, a row that disappeared between the read and the delete is not an error, and the work runs in batches because a store that has never cleaned up could have thousands and a cron that tried to delete them all in one request would time out and delete none. The file goes before the row, because the other order leaves — on a failure between the two — exactly the orphan this job exists to remove and which nothing would ever find again. The job is a single event that reschedules itself rather than a recurring one, so a site that cannot run its cron has at most one occurrence waiting instead of a pile of missed runs. The proof caught its own code: sweep() incremented the tally by the decision rather than the result, creating an `expire` key nobody read and leaving `expired` at zero — the cleanup worked and the count lied, and it was visible only because the assertion prints the tally it observed.

defects_found_and_fixed: The gate observed on demand, so a storefront request that built the checkout's data could make an outbound HTTP request to the store's own address and write an option. Found by the sweep: a proof that asserts the environment is left as it found it counted one more option than it started with. Fixed by splitting reading from observing: enabled() reads a fresh observation and never makes one, and an unobserved environment is unavailable with that as the reason.

Adding the file type to the classic adapter broke six proofs of earlier phases — five that used `file` as their example of an unrenderable type, and four that enumerate the storefront's hooks exactly. All were stale assertions of the world before the change, and all were repointed at what they meant: a structural type, and the new hook named. Recorded rather than quietly patched because it is the recurring cost this project keeps paying: an assertion pinned to a world state fails for the right reason and gets edited for the wrong one.

Four proofs that enumerate the storefront's hooks exactly failed again when this task added its binding hook — the second time in two tasks. Rather than patch four lists a second time, the expected list now lives in tests/Integration/support/storefront-hooks.php and the four read it: the assertion stays a deliberate inventory of what the plugin puts on a storefront request, and a new hook is named once.

The retention sweep incremented its tally by the decision instead of the result, so 'expire' was counted into a key nobody read and 'expired' stayed at zero. The cleanup itself worked — files and rows were removed — and no test would have caught the count, which was visible only because the assertion prints the tally it observed. Third time this session that the printed detail, and not the condition, is what denounced a defect.

The proof's own expectation of how many rows a sweep keeps was wrong: it expected the two survivors, when only the bound one is even a candidate — an upload inside its time is never examined. The assertion now says one and explains why, instead of asserting a number that made the batch look less selective than it is.

F09.title: Página customizada e pagamento
F09.gate: Pedidos reais de sandbox nos cenários homologados, sem inputs de cartão próprios e sem Checkout Sidebar.
F09.why_gate_is_open: Four of the five tasks are complete and one is blocked. The gate is about sandbox orders placed in homologated scenarios — with no checkout collecting card data of its own and no Checkout Sidebar — and the only clause still unmet is the one that needs a gateway: WCCS-049 delivered the homologation matrix and its decision, but its five observations (sandbox, 3DS or redirect, saved tokens, retry, required data) need a gateway enabled with sandbox credentials, which is the blocker SANDBOX-PAYMENT recorded since WCCS-004 and resolvable only outside the plugin root. Of the gate's three clauses, two are asserted over the code: no card input of this plugin's own exists in the type registry, the payment extension points or either module, and the Checkout Sidebar has been out of v1 scope since the planning was captured. The store also has no classic and no Blocks checkout page (CLASSIC-TEST-SURFACE), so nothing has been observed in a browser.
F09.way_forward: One external action closes the phase: enable a gateway in sandbox mode with valid credentials, run the scenarios and write the rows — id, version, mode, tested[] — into resources/payments/homologation.json. Until then every gateway answers 'undecided' and both the checkout and the diagnostics screen say so, which is the honest state and the one the code enforces. F10 may proceed meanwhile: it is the administration work, and it depends on nothing this environment is missing.
F09.detail: WCCS-046 delivered the classic presentation, and the defect it had to fix was its own. The planning records the shape the layout must avoid — a sibling margin between fields misaligning the second element inside a grid — so the spacing is `gap` on the container and on the field wrappers, and the file contains no spacing margin at all. It is asserted as an absence rather than as an override, because a stylesheet that set those margins to zero would still be a stylesheet that had them, and the next person to add a field would inherit the same misalignment one selector later. The unit suite reads the file the way a stylesheet is read: every selector is qualified by the scope, the values are tokens that exist, the focus ring is never removed, the width classes are the ones the adapter emits, and below the narrow breakpoint a three-column field is a full-width one. The scope is where the real defect was. Every selector was written under `.wccs-checkout`, and nothing emitted that class: this plugin ships no template, the theme does not know the name, and WooCommerce's own body class is `woocommerce-checkout`. The stylesheet was written, delivered and applied to nothing, and no unit test could see it because the file is correct as a file — it surfaced when the integration proof asked which half delivers the class and found none. The fix was not to widen the scope onto somebody else's class but to deliver the class through the same gate that delivers the file, so the class is present on exactly the requests that are given the presentation, and on any other request the body classes come back identical to what the theme left. That cost one hook, `body_class`, and it is the only hook this task adds; it is named once in the shared storefront hook list, which exists so a new hook appears in one place to be reviewed instead of in five to be forgotten, and the proof asserts that list equals what the plugin registers. The second half of the acceptance is the word 'hooks preservados', and it is measured three ways: the plugin ships no directory WooCommerce reads templates from, it points no template loader at itself, and it puts nothing on the actions a form is drawn from — a scan run over every class of the plugin rather than one namespace. The fields still reach the form the supported way, filtered into WooCommerce's own field array. The stylesheet is served as its own file rather than injected by the bundle, with the design tokens declared as its dependency so the variables it reads exist before it uses them: a layout that arrives with the JavaScript is a layout the customer does not get until the bundle has run, and on a slow connection that is a checkout arranged differently from the one the merchant approved. Adding the two stylesheets made a proof of an earlier phase fail, and the failure was the useful kind: WCCS-025 asserted that a request which is not the checkout is left with no plugin asset registered, and counted two — the two stylesheets registered by the harness's own earlier section, which exercises the positive path. The intent was right and the measurement was not, so the handles are now cleared before the question is asked instead of the assertion being loosened. The same sweep surfaced the one intermittent failure this file has carried for several phases, WCCS-008 failing fifteen assertions from a single one that demanded a database somebody else had left clean; the file now clears the three options it is about and asserts zero at the end, so it runs in any order. Where the leftover options came from was not identified, and the instrumented sweep that counts the plugin's options after each of the forty-one harnesses shows zero after every one of them; that is recorded as unidentified rather than explained. WCCS-047 delivered the Blocks presentation, and the acceptance decided what the file is allowed to be. The Blocks checkout is WooCommerce's page: the field blocks it draws, the order summary and the whole payment area are markup this plugin did not write and was not promised, and what it is given is a region inside a location. Every selector is therefore written under the wrapper class its own components always render, which makes reaching a WooCommerce field block or a payment component impossible rather than merely unintended — and, unlike the classic presentation one task earlier, that class is emitted by a component that already existed, so there is no scope waiting for a class nobody adds. Both halves of the acceptance are asserted rather than promised. No field is cloned, and it is asserted over the whole registry instead of over examples: a document with one field per registered type is published, both halves answer, and the set the native adapter registered is disjoint from the set the renderer publishes — 21 types, 3 native, 7 controlled, 11 restricted, each claimed by the half its mode names, and a restricted type claimed by anybody fails. No payment component is cloned or restyled, in four absences: the plugin has no callback on either Blocks payment extension point, declares no card or payment field type, promises no payment renderer in any restriction reason, and the stylesheet it serves names payment nowhere. Two decisions are genuinely different from the classic file, and both come from the checkout being different. The responsive rule is a container query rather than a media query, because the same checkout places these fields in a wide column or in a narrow order sidebar and the region, not the window, is what can answer how much room there is — the unit suite requires the container query and forbids any media query in the file. And the design tokens now declare themselves on this scope as well: they lived on the admin screen and the classic checkout, neither of which is on the page here, so the file would have rendered with its fallbacks — the same family of defect WCCS-046 found one checkout over, with a test that reads the token file's selectors and requires this scope. Delivering a stylesheet with the tokens as its declared dependency now exists once, in Checkout\Presentation, so the order that matters is not two implementations that agree today; ClassicAssets was repointed at it unchanged, which its own proof confirms. The proof found two defects in itself, and both are the recurring kind. It called a method that lives on the adapter rather than the renderer, and the harness died with exit 255 and not one line of error — the third silent death of the session, identified with a shutdown handler that prints error_get_last(), and the reason the sweep reads exit codes and not only the RESULT line. And its payment assertion asked whether the payment hook was empty, which is a question about WooCommerce: the hook carries four callbacks, all of the platform's own. Measuring the world instead of the subject is the third time in this session, after the two assets WCCS-025 counted from its own earlier section and the three options WCCS-008 demanded nobody had left; it now asks who is on the hook and which of them is this plugin, and prints the total count beside it so the difference between 'nothing is there' and 'nothing of ours is there' is visible in the output. WCCS-048 delivered the payment accordion and the order summary, and the reading of the installed WooCommerce changed the design of the first one. The module was written to own the accordion state — hiding the panels of the methods that were not chosen — and that was a defect, not a redundancy. checkout/payment-method.php hides the unselected panels itself with an inline style and assets/js/frontend/checkout.js slides them when the radio changes, so a second owner of that state disagrees with the platform in the direction that matters: the panel of a method the customer has just selected, hidden by an attribute the platform's script never touches. The module now wires and does not decide: it gives the gateway's panel an id, points each radio at it with aria-controls, and marks the row so the stylesheet can style a box this plugin did not write. No display, no hidden, no focus(). The stylesheet is asserted not to set display on a panel either, because that is exactly where the defect would come back. 'Real radios' is asserted by counting: the number of inputs is the same before and after and they are the same nodes, a gateway's own card field, nonce and iframe keep their values and their src, the panels' inline styles come out byte for byte identical, and the focus does not move. The integration proof grounds every selector in the platform's own templates read from disk rather than assumed — an invented selector does not fail in jsdom, it fails in production in silence. 'The totals come from WooCommerce' is proven by the module being unable to price anything: the jsdom suite counts the nodes of the page before and after and exactly one is added, the summary's markup comes out identical and its values stay where the store put them; the proof asserts that neither module calls toFixed, Intl.NumberFormat or parseFloat, and that the server payload carries no total, coupons or shipping, because a number that travelled from here would be a second source for it and the second source is the one that goes stale. The one string this task adds — the control's label and its show/hide names — travels from the server in __() with the plugin text domain, so the bundle hardcodes nothing a translator has to find. Keyboard and focus are the platform's: the control is a real button, so Enter and Space are the browser's, the radios are the form's own group, and the spec focuses the button, presses it twice and asserts focus is still there. The layout rules are the ones section 17 records — the payment list and the panel carry margin: 0 and the container carries the gap — and the first version broke that with a margin-block-start on the panel, which the WCCS-046 stylesheet test refused. On a wide page the summary is open and the control is off the page; on a narrow one it starts closed and the control is inserted as a sibling immediately before the summary, never inside it. Whether the page is narrow is handed in as a function so both branches are exercised in jsdom, the same substitution the classic assets use. The task also cost a tooling discovery: wp-scripts format rewrites versioned JSON fixtures as well as JavaScript — 1046 lines of churn in resources/fixtures/conditions.json and a reformat of resources/design-tokens/tokens.json — and both were reverted before the gates were re-run. One thing is named rather than done: section 15 asks for the summary before the form on a narrow page, which is a DOM reordering of a WooCommerce element and is explicitly not to be faked with CSS order, so it stays with the page presentation in WCCS-063. WCCS-049 delivered the payment homologation matrix, and it is deliberately not a compatibility table. Section 15 asks for three things at once — a compatible mode for a gateway that does not tolerate a decoration, an exact record of gateway, version, mode and scenario tested, and no promise of compatibility with every gateway — and the third is the one a table always gets wrong, because somebody writes a mode and nobody asks where the evidence is. The rule here is that a claim needs evidence: a row that declares a mode and names no passing scenario is undecided whatever it says; a scenario outside the record's own vocabulary is discarded, because a test that passed against a scenario nobody wrote down how to run is not evidence; a row recorded for 1.0.0 says nothing about the 2.0.0 installed today, and the decision says so in words rather than promoting a stale run to a promise about different code; and a record that cannot be read is undecided for everything rather than an error or a permission, because a checkout that cannot read the record must fall back to promising nothing and not to promising everything. All four are asserted against a forged record as well as the shipped one, because the rule has to hold for the file somebody writes tomorrow. On this store the answer is the honest one: seven gateways installed, none enabled, all seven undecided, nothing promised — and the payload publishes that alongside the count of gateways nobody ran, so the difference between 'we tested it' and 'we have not looked' is visible to whoever has to act on it. The proof caught a subtlety worth keeping: the payload answers for the gateways the checkout will actually present, not the installed ones, so a store with seven configured and none enabled carries no decision at all and the assertion says installed=7 offered=0 instead of asserting the comfortable equality with the installed list. The record has a consumer, because a record nobody reads is a promise by another name: the decision reaches the payload, the component marks each row with the mode, and a withheld decoration is one the module never applies — it does not write the attribute the stylesheet draws the box from, which is the difference between a record that is honoured and one that is negotiated. Everything else stays wired: the panel id, the aria-controls and the accessibility are untouched, because what a record withholds is a decoration and not a customer's ability to use the field. The decoration vocabulary lists only what the code can withhold today and the proof asserts that with the reason written down: an entry nothing honours would read like a promise. Two things are named rather than done. Express checkout is not integrated — section 15 says a flag on a field does not create an integration, and the security gate it describes can only be verified against a running express gateway — so the 'express' scenario sits in the record's vocabulary as the thing still missing. And the five observations themselves are not made: no gateway is enabled, no credentials exist, and the task is recorded as partially complete and blocked rather than closed. WCCS-050 delivered the opt-in, the diagnostics and the safe return, and its two clauses are assertions by comparison rather than claims. Section 15's first sentence decides the design: the switch is opt-in and off, because a plugin that changes a store's checkout the moment it is activated has taken a decision that belongs to the merchant and cannot be seen until the editor is; an absent option, a stray value and a half-written one all read as off, because the default of a switch that changes a checkout has to be the one that changes nothing. The second half is the sentence that shapes everything else — 'desativação restaura a apresentação original preservando o editor de campos' — and it is proven by comparison: the three schema slots are read raw from the options table before and after a toggle and compared byte for byte, the published field is still there, the engine's types, validators, normalizers, sources and operators are identical, and the switch is one option of its own whose name never appears inside the document. The switch governs the presentation and not the product, which the proof shows from the other side too: opted out, the stylesheet is not enqueued and the field bundle still is, and the payload still carries masks, rules, conditions, uploads and validation. Section 15's other sentence — 'uma incompatibilidade não autoriza trocar silenciosamente a engine da página' — is the safe return: a gateway the homologation record marks unavailable makes this presentation step aside for the store's own checkout, fields and validation included, with the gateway named in the reason so a merchant can act on it. That rule is asserted, the page is asserted to decide with the same rule over the same list, and what cannot be reached is recorded rather than faked: exercising the fallback with a gateway actually offered needs a WC_Payment_Gateway reporting itself available, which is the SANDBOX-PAYMENT blocker again. The last piece is the surface a merchant uses: one route with a read and a write, one screen serving both Settings and Diagnostics because they answer one question between them, and a screen that shows the mode the server decided rather than the switch — the case that matters is the one where they differ, with the opt-in on and a gateway blocking it. The compatibility half is a read with no control at all over it, and one jsdom spec counts the controls to keep it that way: a screen that could write a homologation would be a screen where somebody promises a gateway into compatibility. Two things were found on the way. The first version of the screen imported @wordpress/components; the lint refused it because the admin of this plugin has its own primitives, and a screen bringing a second set would be drawing in two languages. And WCCS-014's assertion that the payload publishes the controllers' route maps verbatim enumerated the two controllers that existed when it was written, so the new route broke it legitimately — instead of adding a third name that would break again at the next controller, the composition moved into Admin\Routes::all(), read by the assets that publish it and by the proof that asserts it, which is the same move the shared storefront hook list got on the day its duplication showed.

defects_found_and_fixed: The presentation stylesheet is written under `.wccs-checkout` and nothing emitted that class: the plugin ships no template, the theme does not know the name and WooCommerce's own body class is `woocommerce-checkout`. The file was written, enqueued and applied to nothing, and no unit test could see it — the file is correct as a file. Found by asking, while writing the integration proof, which half delivers the class, and finding none. Fixed by adding a `body_class` filter that calls the same `should_enqueue()` gate, so the class is on exactly the requests given the presentation and on no others.

WCCS-025's assertion that a non-checkout request is left with no plugin asset registered counted the two stylesheets registered by its own earlier section, which exercises the positive path. The intent was right and the measurement was wrong: it counted the harness's registrations instead of the request's. Fixed by clearing the plugin's handles before asking, not by loosening the assertion.

WCCS-008 failed fifteen assertions in a chain from one that required a database somebody else had left clean, and ended by comparing the final state with that starting value rather than with zero — two assertions about the environment rather than about the code. The file now clears the three options it is about before measuring and asserts zero afterwards, so it passes in any order. The origin of the leftover options was not identified: an instrumented sweep counting the plugin's options after each of the forty-one harnesses shows zero after every one.

phpcs rejected the stylesheet's unit test for three `file_get_contents()` calls. They read local versioned files beside the test, and the sniff targets remote URLs, so the three reads now go through one helper carrying the suppression and its reason once instead of three times.

The Blocks presentation called BlocksRenderer::mode(), which lives on BlocksAdapter. The harness died with exit 255 and no error output at all — the third silent harness death of this session. Found by arming a shutdown handler that prints error_get_last(), because the sweep reads exit codes and a harness that dies quietly would otherwise be counted as one that had nothing to report.

The proof's payment assertion asked whether the Blocks payment extension point had any callbacks, which is a question about WooCommerce: the hook carries four callbacks, all of the platform's own payment methods. Measuring the world instead of the subject is the third occurrence in this session. It now asks who is on the hook and which of them belongs to this plugin, and prints the total count beside the answer.

The proof's closing option count was compared against a value measured at the start, which is whatever a previous run left behind — so a run that died before its cleanup could make the next one fail. The harness now clears the published slot itself before measuring, the same correction WCCS-008's proof received on the same day and for the same reason.

The tokens stylesheet declared the custom properties on the admin scope and the classic checkout scope only, so the new Blocks presentation — which renders on a page where neither exists — would have read every variable as undefined and drawn with its fallbacks. Found while wiring the file, and now asserted by a test that reads the token file's selectors and requires the region scope among them.

The payment accordion owned a state the platform already owns: it set `hidden` on the panels of the methods that were not chosen. checkout/payment-method.php hides the unselected panels with an inline style and assets/js/frontend/checkout.js slides them when the radio changes, so the two owners disagree in the direction that matters — the panel of a method the customer has just selected, hidden by an attribute the platform's script never touches, is a checkout that cannot be paid. Found by reading the installed template instead of assuming how an accordion is built. The module now only wires (an id on the gateway's panel, aria-controls on the radio, a marker on the row), and neither it nor the stylesheet sets visibility on a panel.

The first version of the payment stylesheet set a spacing margin on the gateway's panel — margin-block-start: var(--wccs-checkout-field-gap) — which is precisely the defect section 17 records and which the WCCS-046 stylesheet test refused. Found by that test, on the first run, which is what it exists for. The spacing moved to the container: the payment list carries the gap and every row carries margin: 0.

The payment frame counted a row as prepared when it had merely been found already prepared, so every refresh reported that all methods had been prepared again and the once-per-element promise was unverifiable. Found by a spec asserting the second pass returns zero; the count now distinguishes a row prepared in this pass from one prepared earlier.

The panel lookup inside a payment row could return the radio itself: the walk skipped the label, the script tags and the method class but not the input, so a row with no panel reported one, and prepareMethod answered prepared:true for a panel that was an input element. Found by a spec asserting that a method with no panel is reported rather than invented.

npm run format rewrote two versioned data files — resources/fixtures/conditions.json with 1046 lines of churn and resources/design-tokens/tokens.json — because the formatter covers resources/ and not only JavaScript. Both were reverted and every gate re-run afterwards. Recorded because the next person to run the formatter over resources/ will do the same thing to other tasks' data.

PHPStan refused the guard around the gateway list — `function_exists( 'WC' ) && WC()->payment_gateways()` has a right side that is always true, because the stubs type the accessor as non-nullable. Found by the gate rather than by a failure at runtime; the check is now on the function alone.
phpcs refused four alignment warnings in the new unit suite, which phpcbf fixed; the warnings were formatting only and are recorded because the gate reads exit codes and a warning is a non-zero exit.

WCCS-014's assertion that the bootstrap publishes the controllers' route maps verbatim enumerated the two controllers that existed when it was written, so adding the settings route broke it. The fix is not a third name — that breaks again at the next controller — but a single source for the composition: Admin\Routes::all(), read by the assets that publish the payload and by the proof that asserts it.

The first version of the settings screen imported @wordpress/components, which the lint refused: this plugin's admin has its own primitives (Button, CheckboxField, Notice) and a screen importing another set would be drawing in two languages. Rewritten on the house components.

The opt-in gate was first written to disable the whole checkout bundle, which would have taken the fields down with the presentation — the opposite of the acceptance's 'preserving the editor'. The switch now gates the stylesheet and the two presentation components, and the proof asserts that the field bundle is still delivered with the switch off.

Two PHPStan errors on the way: an always-true right-hand side in the gateway guard, and an unreachable else after a stub says the accessor returns an array. Both are the stubs being right; the checks were removed rather than silenced.

The WCCS-050 proof died silently — exit 255, no output — for the fourth time in this session, because Sources::all() and Operators::all() return keyed maps of value objects and the snapshot cast them to strings. Found with a shutdown handler that prints error_get_last(), which is now the reflex.

F10.title: Pedidos, Minha Conta, APIs e privacidade
F10.gate: Auditoria por papel/endpoint/e-mail confirma ausência de exposição indevida e leitura histórica.
F10.why_gate_is_open: All five of the phase's tasks are complete. The gate asks for an audit — by role, by endpoint and by e-mail, confirming that nothing is exposed that should not be and that history reads correctly — and an audit is an artefact of its own rather than the sum of the authorizations each surface asserts. Every surface does assert its own: the order panel checks the per-order capability, the customer view reads the field's own policy, the e-mails project two audiences and two formats, the integration API answers three refusals and one enumeration oracle, and the data-subject flows read one definition of personal data. Spread across proofs, that is not an audit, and saying so is the honest state of this gate.
F10.way_forward: One artefact closes the phase: a role-by-endpoint matrix, read as a document, that walks every role against every endpoint and every e-mail and states what each may see. It is a reading of what exists rather than new code. F11 is already under way — its first three tasks were delivered while this entry was being corrected to match the planning, which is recorded here rather than smoothed over.
F10.detail: WCCS-051 delivered the checkout fields on the order edit screen. Section 14 asks for four things in one sentence — the block, the origin, the label, the formatted value, authorized editing and a trail of changes — and the panel shows the label as it was when the order was placed rather than the one the field carries today, because a merchant who renames a field has not renamed what a past order says. Authorized editing turned out to be two questions and not one. The first is whether the person may edit this order: manage_woocommerce and edit_shop_order for that order, and a submission carrying a valid nonce still writes nothing without them. The second is whether the order is where that field's value belongs, and it is the one that matters: section 14 separates the order's value from the profile's current preference in one direction — 'editar perfil não reescreve pedido passado' — and read backwards it is what stops this panel, because a field the store keeps on the customer is not editable from one order's snapshot without rewriting a person's current preference from it. The proof publishes four fields and asserts that exactly one is editable. Validation is identical because it is not re-implemented: a value typed here goes through the same ValueProcessor the checkout runs, with the same definitions, and the proof compares the two answers of that one code to four real documents, requiring the accepted value and the canonical value to match and the refusals to be the same. Both order backends are one contract rather than two code paths: the panel registers on add_meta_boxes, which WooCommerce fires with the screen identifier for the legacy posts screen and the HPOS orders screen alike, saves on woocommerce_process_shop_order_meta, which both edit screens fire, and reads and writes only through the WC_Order CRUD. There is one assertion that exists for the day somebody 'fixes' it with update_post_meta(): zero rows in wp_postmeta, because with HPOS authoritative that is the wrong table and a panel writing there would appear to work until the store turned synchronization off. The proof found a real accessibility defect in the panel — a label with a for attribute on every row, including the read-only ones where no control exists, so a screen reader announced a control the keyboard could not reach — and it found a worse defect in itself. The first version asked about validator key br_cpf where the registry declares br.cpf, and the two halves agreed perfectly about a definition no merchant could have saved, because no validation existed: an agreement assertion that was very nearly vacuous and passed. Two structural corrections followed, the cases now use the registry's own keys and the shared fixture's documents, and a guard was added requiring the cases to be decided in both directions before agreeing means anything — 'they agree' that was 'both refuse everything' proves nothing. A third of the same family: the cases were a map with the document as the key, and PHP turns a numeric string key into an integer, so the validation was being asked about an int and refusing it for not being a string. They are explicit pairs now. One thing is named rather than claimed: the trail of changes section 14 also asks for — who changed what in the administration — does not exist yet. WCCS-052 delivered the customer's own view of the order, and reading the installed WooCommerce shaped it: the two components the task names — the thank-you page and My Account — are the same rendering surface, because one renderer is hooked to `woocommerce_thankyou` and to `woocommerce_view_order` and both load the template that fires `woocommerce_order_details_after_order_table`. One hook therefore covers both, and the plugin registers no route, page or shortcode of its own: the hook fires only where the store has already decided this order may be seen by this person, and what this plugin adds is the per-field policy on top of that decision rather than a second access check that would be redundant at best. The acceptance's first clause has three ways to refuse and all three are asserted: the field does not declare `customer_order`, the merchant stopped showing it to the customer, or there is no policy left to read because the field was archived or deleted since the order was placed. That third case is the one worth stating: the order carries the value and the field is gone, and the value is not shown, because the opposite direction shows a customer a document the merchant stopped showing on the strength of a value that happens to be there. With nothing left to show the page renders nothing at all — a heading with no rows tells the customer something was withheld, which is information neither given nor chosen. The second clause is the same separation WCCS-051 asserted for editing, read in the other direction: the proof builds an order that captured one value, puts a different value under the same key on the customer's account, and asserts that the page shows the order's and never the account's — and that an order which captured nothing shows nothing even when the account holds something. No path in the class reads customer meta, the session or the published document for a value: values come from the order's own payload and the label comes from what was recorded with it, so a field renamed today does not rename what a past order says. A stored value is escaped, asserted with markup and quotes stored as the value, because the customer's page is not a place where a stored value becomes markup. One gap is named rather than improvised: values are printed as plain text per type — dates, choices and lists have no formatter yet — and that decision belongs to this phase rather than to this task. WCCS-053 delivered the order e-mails, and the hook carries both answers: `woocommerce_email_order_meta` is fired by every order e-mail template with the order, whether the message goes to the store and whether the text part is being rendered — and WooCommerce uses that hook itself for the customer note, so it is the documented seam rather than one this plugin invented. The four projections are therefore decided from what the platform hands over rather than from a setting that could disagree with the message being sent. Two audiences read two different keys and the proof publishes four fields to show that the sets are not the same set — a field can be in both e-mails, in one, or in neither — and it asserts the case worth stating on its own: a field visible on the customer's order page is in neither e-mail, because a surface is not a policy. Two formats are built and not derived: the HTML part escapes and uses structure, and the text part is written as text, with the assertion made on the value `Salt & pepper bold` — the HTML must not contain the tag as markup and the text must contain neither markup this plugin emitted nor a single entity, because the customer's own angle brackets are their text and `&` in a plain-text e-mail is the defect the split exists to prevent. Documents are never attached: the plugin adds nothing to `woocommerce_email_attachments`, asserted by looking for this plugin's callbacks on every hook whose name contains it rather than by asking whether the filter is empty — which would be a question about WooCommerce, and is the fourth time in this session that pattern has had to be corrected. A link exists only when a store configures one through the filter this class publishes, and then it is the plugin's own authorization route, the one that decides per request whether this person may read this file, and never a path, a public URL or an address into `wp-content`. The proof found a real defect while asserting the other direction: with links configured, a value that is not a token produced an anchor with an empty href — something that looks like a way to the document, is focusable and goes nowhere. The correction reordered the decisions, address first and link second: no address, no link, only the sentence that names the document. PHPStan then refused a docblock that said `entries()` returns entries when it returns pairs — the entry and the definition that authorised it, because a document is rendered by its definition and not by its value — and the annotation was corrected rather than silenced. One thing is named: the screen where a merchant turns controlled links on does not exist, so the filter is exercised and the configuration is not yet reachable. WCCS-054 delivered the integration API, and the acceptance's second clause is what shaped it: the route lives in the plugin's own namespace and never on the Store API's, because the Store API is the surface an anonymous browser reaches during checkout while an integration is a caller that has authenticated and been authorized per order — putting them in one namespace would make them indistinguishable in a log, in a firewall rule and in a reviewer's head. Section 14's list is honoured clause by clause: every route declares its args with a description and a type, the page size has a maximum, the identifier is validated before it reaches a query, the collection is paged and reports its total, and the projection is an allow list built from the published fields and the order's own payload rather than a dump of the order's meta — no meta key appears in a response. Authorization is exercised against the real REST server with real users rather than as return values: an anonymous caller is refused with the unauthenticated code, an authenticated customer without the capability with the forbidden one, and a caller who may read orders but not a particular order is refused as well, because 'may read orders' and 'may read this customer's order' are different sentences. The proof found a defect in the design it was testing: a missing order and a foreign one returned different codes, which is precisely the enumeration oracle the class docblock claimed to avoid — anybody who may read orders could have counted the store's orders by asking for identifiers and watching which answer came back. The refusal is now one code for both cases, decided before the order is even resolved, and the trade-off is written down: a caller asking for a deleted order is told it is not allowed rather than that it does not exist. The second clause is asserted against the platform's own public route: an order carrying both an exposed and a private value is requested through the installed Store API with its order key, exactly as a visitor would, and the response is asserted to contain no field identifier, no underscore-prefixed meta key, and neither value — with a guard asserting the Store API actually answered, so 'it does not contain' is not a statement about nothing. The only Store API extension the plugin makes remains the type contract WCCS-038 registered, which a test reads the file to confirm. The harness itself died silently for the fifth time in this session when the first version expected a WP_Error from a permission refusal; rest_do_request returns the refusal as a response, and the assertions now read the status and the code the server actually sends. One gap is named rather than improvised: the contract is declared and readable on the server, but no API document for an integrator exists yet. WCCS-055 delivered the two data-subject flows and the policy text. The flows are registered on WordPress's own privacy filters and the proof reaches them through those filters, because an exporter registered where nobody reads it does not exist for the person asking. What counts as personal data is not a list written in the class: it is the storage sensitivity vocabulary the merchant configured, where `personal` identifies a person and `sensitive` is a document needing extra care, while `public` identifies nobody on its own and is therefore left out of the export. Both callbacks read that one decision, because a person told their data is one thing when they ask for a copy and another when they ask for it to be gone has been told two different things by one store. Finding the orders is the part that is easy to get wrong quietly, so it is done both ways — by billing address and by customer identifier — and the proof builds the case that a search by address alone misses: a person with a guest order under one address and an account order under another, whose second order must be erased too. `wc_get_orders()` is used rather than a query because that is the call both order backends answer, and a privacy tool reading the wrong table would tell a person their data does not exist. The erasure erases the values and not the order, on section 14's own reasoning about refunds and cancellations; it sets `items_retained` with the reason written out, which is the acceptance's 'retenção explicável' — a flow that silently keeps something is a flow nobody can explain to the person who asked; and a document bound to an existing order is named rather than deleted from here, because that file is part of the order's record while the order exists and the store's own upload retention removes it with the order. Running the erasure twice is safe, which is what a person retrying the tool needs. The policy is generated rather than written: the sensitivity and visibility vocabularies supply what each kind of value means and where it appears, and the retention numbers are read from the constants the retention job actually uses, so the number in the policy is the number in the code. Hand-written policy text is the document nobody updates, and it drifts in the direction that matters because the policy is what the person reads. The last paragraph states that the text is not legal advice and claims no conformity with any law, with an assertion refusing the phrases that would claim it — section 14 forbids 'uma promessa genérica de conformidade'. Two things are named rather than resolved: whether the person is entitled to the document itself and by what route is a store policy decision still open — the export says a document exists and does not hand over the internal address — and how long an effective order is kept is still not a setting. The proof passed on its first run, which is the second time in this session and is recorded as the exception.

defects_found_and_fixed: The order panel emitted a `<label for="...">` on every row, including the read-only ones where no control is drawn: the for attribute pointed at an element that does not exist, which a screen reader announces as a control and a keyboard cannot reach. Found by the assertion that the customer-scoped field is shown without a control to change it; the read-only row is a span now and the label only exists where the input does.

The proof's first version compared the checkout's pipeline with the panel's using validator key `br_cpf` where the registry declares `br.cpf`. Both sides agreed perfectly — about a definition no merchant could have saved, because no validation existed. An agreement assertion that was very nearly vacuous and passed. Found while chasing a value that was supposed never to be refused; the cases now use the registry's keys and the shared fixture's documents, and a guard requires them to be decided in both directions before agreeing means anything.

The proof's cases were a map whose keys were the documents, and PHP converts a numeric string array key into an integer, so the validation was asked about an `int` and refused it for not being a string. Found by the same guard, which printed the verdicts; the cases are explicit pairs now.

phpcs refused the order capabilities as unknown, which is true of a sniff that cannot know what WooCommerce registers at runtime. Taught to the same configuration block that already teaches it `manage_woocommerce`, with the reason written beside it.
The panel's render parameter was named `object`, a reserved word the standard refuses. Renamed to the thing the screen actually passes.

The e-mail projection emitted an anchor with an empty href when controlled links were configured and the value was not a token this store holds: something that looks like a way to the document, is focusable, and goes nowhere. Found by the assertion that a value which is not a token produces no address; the correction put the address decision before the link, so no address means no link.

PHPStan refused a docblock in the new projection that declared `entries()` returns `OrderFieldEntry` when it returns pairs of entry and definition — five errors in cascade. The annotation was lying about the shape that a document's rendering depends on; corrected, not silenced.

phpcs refused four unescaped outputs in the text part of the e-mail. Escaping there is the defect the format split exists to prevent, so the suppressions carry the reason in the same line — the standard this project uses for the sniffs that cannot see through a call or a constant.

The attachment check was first written as `has_filter( 'woocommerce_email_attachments' )`, which asks whether WooCommerce or another plugin attaches anything — the fourth occurrence in this session of measuring the world instead of the subject. It now looks for this plugin's own callbacks on every hook whose name contains it.

The integration API returned `wccs_unknown_order` for an identifier that does not exist and `wccs_forbidden_order` for an order that is not the caller's, which is an enumeration oracle: anybody who may read orders could count the store's orders by asking for identifiers and watching which of the two answers came back. Found by the assertion that both must be refused the same way. There is one refusal code now, decided before the order is resolved, and the trade-off — a deleted order reads as 'not allowed' — is recorded in the class.

The proof died silently a fifth time in this session: the first version expected a `WP_Error` from a permission refusal, and `rest_do_request()` returns a response that carries the refusal. The assertions read the status and the code the server sends, which is what a client sees.
phpcs refused five alignment warnings in the new controller, which phpcbf fixed; recorded because the gate reads exit codes and a warning is a non-zero exit.

Nothing was fixed in this task: the proof passed on its first run, the second time in this session. The one correction on the way was a constant that did not exist — the policy quoted `UploadsRetention::TEMPORARY_TTL` where the temporary upload's life is `UploadService::TTL` — found by reading the class before writing, which is why the policy's number is now the number the retention job uses.
